new_statements.rule_in_words: Korowai word stress is lexical: its position cannot be predicted from the shape of the word and it distinguishes words (dámo 'say, inform' vs damó 'close'); stressed vowels (and open final vowels) are lengthened, unstressed non-final vowels tend to reduce. de Vries (2020, sec. 2.4.3) restates it as 'Word stress is a contrastive pitch accent.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing found (a search for 'secondary stress' in the book returned no hit); the vocabulary marks only the main word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Morphology: 'main stress in perfect forms of the verb is on the verb stem' (with vowel reduction when stress does not fall on the stem-final syllable); stress in compound nouns is likewise unpredictable; schwa is epenthetic and never stressed (per Wikipedia's rendering of the same source). Authors leave stress unmarked on vocabulary items where they were uncertain.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (citation forms; stress written with an acute in ch. 2 and by underlining in the Korowai-English vocabulary; the practical orthography does not mark stress). Realisation: van Enk & de Vries 1997 treat it as dynamic stress with vowel lengthening; de Vries 2020 calls it a contrastive pitch accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Korowai proper (khe, koro1312) as recorded by van Enk (mission linguist) and de Vries; Glottolog/de Vries et al. 2012 treat North Korowai (upper Becking River) as a separate Becking-Dawi variety not covered by this statement.
